newsitem.title: FRANCE: French fire probe clears Eurotunnel - head.
newsitem.headline: French fire probe clears Eurotunnel - head.

text.p: A French judicial probe into a fire which seriously damaged a section of the Channel Tunnel last November has cleared Anglo-French operator Eurotunnel, the executive chairman said on Sunday.
"Neither Eurotunnel nor the lorry company is responsible," Patrick Ponsolle told Europe 1 radio.
A fire broke out on a lorry on a Shuttle freight wagon operated by Eurotunnel SA/Plc on November 18, causing severe damage and disrupting passenger and freight services in the first half of the year.
Ponsolle said that a judicial inquiry into the causes of the fire would be made public in the near future but he refused to be drawn on whether it was an act of arson.
"One is never immune from criminal acts," he said.
But the inquiry had already shown that Eurotunnel's installations and systems were not to blame for the fire, he said.
Some 700,000 Eurotunnel shareholders are due to vote next Thursday on a plan to restructure the company's 70 billion francs of junior-ranked bank debt.
Ponsolle said that institutional investors were backing the refinancing and reiterated his confidence that the required majority of small shareholders would also approve the debt deal.
But the big concern would be whether there would be a quorum of the 25 percent of the total shares, he said. "The important thing is to vote," whether for or against, he said.
If there were no quorum next Thursday, the company would organise another shareholders meeting, he said.
If, at that third meeting, there were still no quorum or the vote went against the restructuring plan, Ponsolle, asked whether he would resign, responded, "I will draw the consequences."
Ponsolle has repeatedly said the company would go into bankruptcy if the shareholders did not back the debt deal, which is needed to ensure its survival.

Eurotunnel's hopes of securing shareholder approval won support last week when the French and British governments agreed conditionally to extend its operating licence by 34 years to at least 99 years.
But that extension depended on getting the refinancing approved, increasing rail freight traffic and a 25 percent share of Eurotunnel's net profits from 2052.

Ponsolle said the new British Labour government under Tony Blair and the Transport Minister and Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott had been more open to Europtunnel's request for an extension than the previous conservative administration under John Major.
Eurotunnel needs to refinance its debt owed to 174 lenders as its revenues fall short of paying its massive interest payments.
But the loan restructuring involves diluting the shareholders' capital to 54.5 percent of the equity base, with the issue of new stock to the banks in exchange for eight billion francs of debt.
